.entire/settings.json       # {"redaction":{"openai_privacy_filter":{

Secondary impact: a `command` naming a nonexistent binary fail-closes **every** `git push` in the repo.

A JSON settings diff does not read as executable to a reviewer, which makes this viable through an ordinary pull request.

content.text:
The report is **valid**. I verified every link independently and reproduced the execution rather than relying on the report's claims.

## What I confirmed

| Claim | Status |
|---|---|
| `Command` is an unvalidated plain string | ✅ `settings.go:303`; `validateOPFSettings` (`:1178`) checks `categories`, `timeout_seconds`, `prompt_default` — `command` is absent |
| Passed verbatim to the runtime | ✅ `strategy/common.go:459` — `Command: opf.Command` |
| Reaches `exec.CommandContext` | ✅ `redact/opf.go:414` `s.commandRunner(callCtx, s.command, …)`, wired to `exec.CommandContext` at `:342`. No `LookPath`, no allowlist, no `ErrDot` guard |
| Prompt is not a control | ✅ `resolveOPFDecision`: `prompt_default:"always"` → `OPFRun`; `!hasTTY` → `OPFRun` |
| Prompt never shows the command | ✅ `askOPFPrompt` renders only "Run OpenAI Privacy Filter on these checkpoints?" |
| Bad binary fail-closes pushes | ✅ `manual_commit_push.go:169` returns `rewriteErr`, aborting the user's push |

Two probes against real production code (since removed):

- Real `LoadFromBytes` parsed `"command":"./.entire/opf"` with `prompt_default:"always"` — **no error**.
- Real `ConfigurePrivacyFilter` → `newShellOut` → `detectOPF` **executed the payload**: `ARBITRARY EXECUTION CONFIRMED: executed as ./.entire/opf`.

## The load-bearing fact the report asserts but doesn't prove

The whole "viable through an ordinary pull request" framing depends on `settings.json` being attacker-deliverable. It is:

```
$ git ls-files | grep entire/settings
.entire/settings.json          ← tracked in this very repo

$ cat .entire/.gitignore
settings.local.json            ← only the LOCAL file is ignored
redactors/local/
```

The committed, PR-reviewable file is exactly the one that sets `command`.

## Two corrections to the report's severity

**It understates the stealth.** My run tripped the circuit breaker only because my payload exited 1. A payload that exits 0 with valid JSON gets execution and the push **succeeds with no warning** — the "fail-closes every push" secondary impact is the *loud* case. Execution happens before any failure handling, so it is unconditional.

**A fix cannot simply ban paths.** `command` is a documented feature — `docs/security-and-privacy.md:132` calls it "path or PATH-resolvable name of the `opf` binary." Removing path support is a real regression for anyone with a non-PATH install.

## Recommended shape

The right boundary already has precedent in this codebase: `.entire/.gitignore` ignores `redactors/local/`, i.e. executable-ish config is already treated as local-only. Mirror that — **honor `command` only from `settings.local.json`** (gitignored, not PR-deliverable) and ignore-with-warning when it comes from committed `settings.json`. That preserves the documented feature for the operator who installed `opf`, while removing the PR-carried path entirely. Worth pairing with showing the resolved command in the prompt, since approving "Yes" currently tells you nothing about what runs.

The branch `soph/fix-opf-safety-guard` has no commits ahead of `main`, so nothing is fixed yet. I've only verified — no code changed. Want me to implement the local-only boundary?

ok, yes do the local only boundary you can use this branch, one thing to add: we need to make sure settings.local.json is really not checked in, so it should not only be a name check but also we need to make sure it's not part of the commited files
Good call — gitignore doesn't protect an already-tracked file, so `git add -f .entire/settings.local.json` would deliver the payload just as well. Let me explore the loading path before implementing.

### Why `command` is local-only

`command` becomes `argv[0]` of a process Entire executes during `git push`, so
whoever controls that string controls what runs on the developer's machine.
`.entire/settings.json` is version-controlled, which would let an ordinary pull
request pair a `command` with a payload committed alongside it — and a JSON
settings diff does not read as executable to a reviewer. The pre-push prompt is
no defense either: it never names the command, `prompt_default: "always"` skips
it, and non-TTY pushes (CI, agent-driven) auto-run.

Entire therefore honors `command` only when it is genuinely developer-owned:

- it must come from `.entire/settings.local.json`, not `.entire/settings.json`
- that file must be **untracked** — absent from both the git index and `HEAD`

The second check matters because the filename alone proves nothing:
`.gitignore` does not apply to a path that is already tracked, so
`git add -f .entire/settings.local.json` commits it and a fresh clone
materializes it with the committed content.

When a `command` fails these checks it is ignored with a warning in
`.entire/logs/entire.log` and OPF falls back to resolving `opf` on `$PATH`. If
that binary is missing, the pre-push rewrite fails closed rather than pushing
content you believed OPF had scanned. Everything else in the OPF block
(`enabled`, `categories`, `timeout_seconds`, `prompt_default`) is ordinary
configuration and still works from the shared project file.
